text:
U.N. talks on regulating AI-powered killer robots ended without a negotiating mandate Saturday, as countries decided to extend discussions until 2028.
Countries party to the U.N.'s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons spent five days in Geneva trying to reach an accord to elaborate legally binding rules for weapons that can select and attack targets without human approval.
But resistance from several countries, and especially Russia, blocked those efforts. In the end, the 128 member countries agreed to launch "the elaboration of an international instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems," over the next two years, Julien Thöni, the Swiss diplomat who chaired the talks, told reporters.
The issue is of growing importance as AI gains new capabilities and autonomous systems become increasingly powerful. Ukraine, Russia, Israel and others are using drones and robots in warfare, although they insist that humans still have ultimate control over pulling the trigger.
However, Stop Killer Robots, a global coalition of more than 300 organizations, said such systems have already been tested or deployed, including in Ukraine and Gaza.
“Autonomous weapons technology, including AI in the targeting cycle, is being deployed on the battlefield — delaying the creation of a legally binding instrument puts civilians and humanity at risk,” said Nicole van Rooijen , the executive director of Stop Killer Robots.
Because consensus is required for any decision, Russia was able to block formal negotiations all week, refusing to allow observers — including the European Union — to take part in the talks. Instead, negotiations were held informally to circumvent Russia’s veto.
A Brazilian diplomat suggested it wasn't only Russia trying to block the effort. “You can blame Russia, but they are not the only ones. Some people are hiding behind Russia,” the diplomat said.
Two EU diplomats listed the U.S., the U.K., South Korea, Japan, Turkey and Israel as countries also resisting an effort to agree on a binding regulation.
In an effort to find a consensus, France called for a "hybrid document" — with both non-binding and binding elements. Germany advocated for an "international instrument" as opposed to a legally binding protocol.
In the final hours of the conference, countries pushing for a regulation on autonomous lethal systems, such as Ireland, Brazil, Belgium and Austria, watered down their positions out of fear of “leaving the conference empty-handed,” the Brazilian diplomat said. They settled for further talks, without calling to adopt a legally binding treaty by 2028.
The final decision seen by POLITICO proposes to “elaborate” an instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems in the context of international humanitarian law. A group of intergovernmental experts should report its conclusions to a 2028 meeting of countries party to the treaty.
As AI and automation transform warfare, civil society groups said the conference fell short of expectations.
“This outcome is disappointing. It does not provide the urgent action needed to agree new rules, but the technology is racing ahead," said Verity Coyle, deputy director for arms at Human Rights Watch.
With no mention of a legally binding instrument in the decision, “it remains possible — likely, even — that there will be no treaty by the end of 2028," said Rain Liivoja, a director with the Asia-Pacific Institute for Law and Security.
